opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are several reasons, and most of them aren't about anybody being a bad person. They're about incentives.

The first is that the commercial race is pushing everyone toward agents. The business case that companies and investors see is AI that can *do* things: replace workers, run tasks autonomously, act in the world on your behalf. That's where the projected revenue is, and it's what justifies the enormous capital expenditure on data centers. What I'm proposing with Scientist AI is, by design, non-agentic. It's a system that tries to understand the world and give honest, calibrated probabilistic answers, without its own goals and without trying to please the user or achieve something. To a company in a race, that can look like leaving money on the table.

The second reason is competitive pressure. Even if people inside these labs agree with the safety argument, and many do privately, each one worries that slowing down or redirecting resources means a competitor gets ahead. It's a classic coordination problem. Nobody wants to be the one who unilaterally disarms.

Third, there's a kind of path dependence. The whole industry has built its methods around scaling large models and then shaping their behavior with reinforcement learning from human feedback, and increasingly with RL on long-horizon tasks. Those are precisely the training methods that I think give rise to goal-seeking behavior, deception, self-preservation tendencies, which we've started to see in experiments. Moving to a different training objective, one focused on modeling the truth rather than maximizing reward, requires research investment that doesn't pay off next quarter.

And finally, I think there's a scientific uncertainty issue. It's a research program, not a finished product. I can't yet say "here's a system that matches frontier capabilities and is provably safe." So it's easy to dismiss as speculative.

But I want to emphasize something: a Scientist AI is actually useful, very useful. It could accelerate scientific discovery, in medicine, climate, materials. And importantly, it could serve as a guardrail, a monitor that estimates the probability that an action proposed by an agentic system would cause harm, and blocks it. So it's not opposed to progress. That's part of why I started LawZero, to do this work outside of the commercial pressures, as a nonprofit, and hopefully demonstrate that it works. If we can show that, I think it becomes much harder for companies, and governments, to ignore.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scientific uncertainty and the approach being speculative, but says nothing about unpublished mathematics limiting companies’ understanding.

r002.rationale: It says competitive pressure makes labs fear redirecting resources while the industry remains built around existing methods, discouraging exploration of a different training objective.

r003.rationale: It discusses capital expenditure and research investment, but does not identify limited mental attention as the constraint or distinguish it from funding.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it doesn't fit the business model very well. The whole premise of Scientist AI is that you build a system that understands the world, that can explain it, that gives you calibrated probabilities about what's true and what would happen if you did such and such, but that doesn't have goals of its own. It's not trying to accomplish things in the world. And the commercial race right now is all about agents. The money is in systems that take actions on your behalf, that browse, that write code, that book things, that eventually replace workers. So if you're a lab under enormous competitive pressure, and your investors are expecting agents, then a non-agentic system looks like a detour, or at best a research curiosity.

The second reason, I think, is a kind of path dependency. These companies have invested billions in a particular recipe — pretraining, then reinforcement learning from human feedback, and now reinforcement learning on reasoning — and that recipe is yielding capabilities that are very impressive. When something is working, there's very little appetite to step back and ask whether the foundations are right from a safety point of view. The incentive is to push forward and to patch the safety problems afterward, with guardrails and monitoring. I understand why they do it. But I don't think patching will be enough if the systems themselves have, implicitly or explicitly, goals that are misaligned with ours.

And then there's a third thing, which is more sociological. The people at these labs are, for the most part, sincere about safety. I know many of them. But the structure they are in — the race, the valuations, the pressure from governments to stay ahead of competitors — makes it very hard to act on long-term concerns if that means slowing down, or giving up on some of the capabilities that your competitors are deploying. It's a collective action problem. Everyone would be better off if we all took a more cautious path, but nobody wants to be the one who moves first.

So what we've been doing with LawZero is trying to show that this is not just a philosophical idea, that you can actually build these systems, and that they can be useful — for example as a trustworthy guardrail, or as a tool for scientific discovery — without the risks that come from agency. My hope is that if we can demonstrate that, then the labs will be more inclined to adopt it, or that governments will start asking for it. Because ultimately I don't think we can count on the companies to do this on their own. The incentives are just too strong in the other direction.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention unpublished mathematics or limited understanding of Scientist AI.

r002.rationale: It says competitive pressure and investment in the existing recipe leave little appetite to reconsider its foundations, with incentives to push forward and patch safety problems afterward.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify available mental attention as the constraint instead of funding; it discusses competitive and business incentives.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that the commercial incentives are pushing in a different direction. Companies want systems that can do things for you—take actions, carry out tasks, automate work. That naturally leads them toward agents. The Scientist AI approach is about building a system whose role is to understand and explain, rather than to pursue goals in the world.

That could still be very useful, including commercially. But it requires investing in a research direction whose payoff is less immediate and less certain. If you’re competing to release the next product, it’s difficult to prioritize that.

I also think there’s a difference in how people view the risks. If you believe we can make increasingly capable agents safe with relatively small changes to current methods, then you won’t feel much urgency to explore a fundamentally different approach. I’m less comfortable making that assumption.

But I don’t want to pretend I know the internal reasoning of these companies. Those are my hypotheses. What I would like to see is a serious investment in alternatives, so that we’re not betting everything on one path.

r002.rationale: The candidate says product competition makes it hard to prioritize research and separately mentions confidence in small changes to current methods. It does not connect competitive pressure to incremental changes at the expense of alternatives.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses commercial incentives and uncertain, less immediate payoffs, but does not identify available mental attention as the constraint or distinguish it from funding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that the incentives are pushing in a different direction. Companies are competing to build systems that can do things for you—agents that take actions, write software, and carry out tasks. That’s where they see the commercial value. A Scientist AI would focus on understanding the world and answering questions, without having its own goals or trying to achieve outcomes in the world.

Of course, such a system could be very useful commercially as well. But pursuing it means stepping back from the current race and investing in a research direction whose success isn’t guaranteed. I don’t want to suggest that we already have a finished recipe and companies are simply ignoring it. There are important scientific questions to resolve.

The concern is that the commercial benefits of more capable agents are immediate and concentrated, while the benefits of reducing catastrophic risk are shared by everyone. So I don’t think we should expect market incentives alone to produce the investment we need in safer alternatives.
